summary: After a day of questions, Jesus asks one: how can the Christ be David’s Son when David, in Psalm 110, calls Him “Lord”? No one can answer.
key_insight: All day the leaders questioned Jesus; now He asks the last question, and it is about Himself. The scribes were right that the Christ is David’s Son. Psalm 110 shows He is also David’s Lord, seated at God’s right hand. Only One who is both David’s descendant and more than a man fits both.
story: While the Pharisees were still gathered together, {Mt} and as He taught in the temple, {Mk} Jesus asked them, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose Son is He?” They said to Him, “The Son of David.” {Mt}

Then He asked how David, speaking by the Holy Spirit, could call Him ‘Lord.’ {Mk} For David himself said in the Book of Psalms, {Lk} “The LORD said to my Lord, ‘Sit at My right hand, Till I make Your enemies Your footstool.’ ”
“If David then calls Him ‘Lord,’ how is He his Son?” {Mt}
No one was able to answer Him a word, and from that day on no one dared question Him anymore. {Mt} But the common people heard Him gladly. {Mk}
differences: In Matthew, Jesus questions the Pharisees directly and they answer, “The Son of David.” In Mark and Luke, He raises the question about what the scribes say, and no reply is recorded.
Matthew says David spoke “in the Spirit,” Mark “by the Holy Spirit,” and Luke “in the Book of Psalms.”
Matthew ends with no one daring to question Jesus again; Mark, who notes that earlier (12:34), ends instead with “the common people heard Him gladly.”

scene.label: Psalm 110
scene.text: The psalm’s title reads “A Psalm of David,” and Jesus’ hearers did not dispute that David wrote it or that it spoke of the Messiah. It is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament passage (for example Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13).

scene.label: LORD and Lord
scene.text: In Hebrew the first “LORD” is God’s personal name, which the NKJV prints in capitals. The second is adon, a title for a master or superior. David pictures God speaking to someone David himself calls master.

scene.label: Fathers and sons
scene.text: In Israel a son honored his father, and a descendant honored the great ancestor of his house. No father called his own descendant “my lord.” That is the knot Jesus sets before the scribes: David’s Son is also David’s Lord.

scene.label: At the right hand
scene.text: The right hand of a king was the seat of honor and shared rule; Solomon set his mother’s throne at his right hand (1 Kings 2:19). To sit at God’s right hand is to share God’s throne. Within days Jesus would tell the high priest that he would see “the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power” (Matthew 26:64).

witnesses.matthew: Makes this the last exchange of the day’s debates: Jesus asks, the Pharisees give half the truth, and no one dares question Him again. Matthew’s Gospel opens with Jesus Christ, “the Son of David” (1:1); here Jesus shows that title is true but not the whole truth.
witnesses.mark: Has Jesus raise the question while teaching in the temple, aimed at what the scribes teach, and ends with His hearers: “the common people heard Him gladly.” Right after, Mark records Jesus’ warning, “Beware of the scribes” (12:38).
witnesses.luke: Places the question right after some scribes praised His answer to the Sadducees, and names the source, “the Book of Psalms.” Luke returns to this psalm in Peter’s sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:34–36), where the risen Jesus is the Lord at God’s right hand.

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims to be more than David’s heir. He is David’s Lord, the One whom God invites to sit at His right hand: truly human through David’s line, and more than human.
seeing.living: Jesus does not let anyone settle for a Messiah who is only a great man from a royal family. He still asks, “What do you think about the Christ?” Answer with the whole truth: He is Lord, seated at God’s right hand, and that claims your obedience, not only your respect.
seeing.ponder: If David called Him “Lord,” is Jesus your Lord, or only someone you admire?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus is David’s Son and David’s Lord, and no one can avoid His question.
preaching.watch_for: All day others had questioned Jesus (21:23; 22:17, 28, 36). Now He asks the final question, and it is about Himself. Psalm 110:1 returns at His trial, where Jesus applies it to Himself before the high priest (26:64).
